title: The Gridiron Beside the School
bigQuestion: How did rough games on college lawns turn into a written game with a governing body and a field every town could build?

story.title: Painted Grass on a Friday
story.kicker: Before anyone sits down, the bleachers face a rectangle of painted grass.
paragraphs: It is Friday afternoon in a small Illinois town. Maya helps her grandfather carry a cooler to the high school field. The bleachers are empty. They all face a long rectangle of grass with white lines painted across it every five yards.

"Why so many lines?" Maya asks. Her grandfather says the lines are old. College rule makers added lines like them in the 1880s. From the stands, the field looked like a cooking grill. People began calling it a gridiron.

A metal sign by the gate says the field belongs to the school district. Taxes and bond votes paid for the grass, the lights and the seats. On game nights the band, the families and the whole town come here.

Maya's grandfather remembers his own school days. Back then, Illinois had no state football playoffs. The Illinois High School Association, called the IHSA, started them in 1974. Now teams from the whole state chase one title each fall.
story.think: Who do you think paid for the field, the lights and the bleachers, and why would a town want one?

lessons.title: Town Games in Old England
lessons.mainIdea: Long before rule books, English towns played huge, rough ball games in the streets, and leaders sometimes banned them.
reading: In medieval England, whole villages played *folk football*. Hundreds of people chased one ball through streets and fields. The goals could be a mile apart. There was no written rule book, and each town had its own customs.

The games were so wild that leaders tried to stop them. In 1314, the Lord Mayor of London banned football in the city in the name of King Edward II. Later kings passed more bans. The games kept going anyway.

Many towns played on *Shrove Tuesday*, a holiday before the Christian season of Lent. The town of Ashbourne in Derbyshire still holds a two-day Shrovetide game. Its two goals stand about three miles apart.

words.d: an old town ball game with many players and no written rules
a holiday before Lent, when many English towns held a big ball game

lessons.title: Rutgers and Princeton, 1869
lessons.mainIdea: The first game between two American colleges was played in New Brunswick, New Jersey, on November 6, 1869.
reading: On November 6, 1869, students from *Rutgers* and Princeton met on a field in New Brunswick, New Jersey. It was the first football game between two American colleges. Each side had 25 players.
The game looked more like soccer than today's American football. Players kicked and batted a round ball. They could not pick it up and run. Rutgers won, six goals to four.
About a hundred people watched. The Rutgers student newspaper, the *Targum*, wrote a report of the game. That report is one reason historians know the date and the score.

words.d: a college in New Jersey that played Princeton in the first college football game, 1869
the Rutgers student newspaper that reported the 1869 game

lessons.title: McGill Visits Harvard, 1874
lessons.mainIdea: In 1874 Harvard played McGill University of Montreal and liked McGill's rugby-style game, which let players carry the ball.
reading: In May 1874, a team from *McGill University* in Montreal, Canada, came to Cambridge, Massachusetts. They played two games against Harvard. McGill played a game like *rugby*, where players could pick up the ball and run.
The two schools split the rules. One game used Harvard's rules. The other used McGill's. Harvard players liked carrying the ball, so they kept the rugby style.
Harvard then played Yale in 1875 using rules close to rugby. Other eastern colleges soon followed. A game from Canada and England had changed the American college game.

words.d: a university in Montreal, Canada, whose team played Harvard in 1874
a football game from England where players may carry the ball

lessons.title: A Meeting at the Massasoit House
lessons.mainIdea: In 1876 college students met in Springfield, Massachusetts, and started the Intercollegiate Football Association with rugby-based rules.
reading: In November 1876, students from four colleges met in Springfield, Massachusetts. They came from Harvard, Yale, Princeton and Columbia. The meeting was held at the Massasoit House hotel. They wanted one set of rules for games between their schools.
The meeting started the *Intercollegiate Football Association*. It was a group of colleges that agreed on shared rules. The group used the rugby rules of England as its base.

Rugby rules then put 15 players on each side. Yale's students wanted fewer players. That argument went on for a few years. It shows that a *convention*, a meeting to agree on rules, did not settle every question at once.

words.d: a group of colleges formed in 1876 to share one set of football rules
a meeting where people agree on rules

lessons.title: Walter Camp's Lines
lessons.mainIdea: Walter Camp of Yale led rule changes in 1880 and 1882 that turned a rugby-style game into American football and gave the field its gridiron lines.
reading: *Walter Camp* played for Yale and later guided its team. He sat on college rule committees for many years. In 1880 his group cut each side to 11 players. It also replaced rugby's scrum with a *line of scrimmage*, where each play starts.
In 1882 a new rule said a team had three tries, called downs, to gain five yards. Officials needed to measure the ground. So lines were drawn across the field every five yards.
From above, the lines looked like a cooking grill, or gridiron. The name stuck. Camp is often called the father of American football. He also wrote a book called American Football in 1891.

words.d: a Yale player and rule maker who shaped American football in the 1880s
the line where each play in American football begins

lessons.title: William Henry Lewis, All-America
lessons.mainIdea: In 1892 William Henry Lewis became the first Black player named to college football's All-America team.
reading: *William Henry Lewis* was born in Virginia in 1868. His parents had been enslaved. He studied at Amherst College and then at Harvard Law School. He played football at both schools.

Starting in 1889, sports writers picked an *All-America team*, a list of the best college players. Walter Camp helped choose it. In 1892 Lewis was named to the list. He was the first Black player chosen.

Few Black students could attend these colleges then. Lewis later became a lawyer. In 1911 he was named an Assistant Attorney General of the United States. He was one of the first Black Americans to hold such a high federal post.

words.d: the first Black player named to the college All-America team, in 1892
a yearly list of the best college football players, begun in 1889

lessons.title: The Hard Season of 1905
lessons.mainIdea: Many players were badly hurt or killed in 1905, and President Theodore Roosevelt pushed colleges to make football safer.
reading: By 1905, college football was a dangerous game. Players crashed together in big piles. Few wore helmets. Newspapers counted about 18 player deaths that season. Many more players were badly hurt.

Some leaders wanted to end football. Columbia University dropped the game in 1905. In October 1905, President *Theodore Roosevelt* invited men from Harvard, Yale and Princeton to the White House. He asked them to make the game safer.

In November 1905, Harold Moore of Union College died in a game against New York University. Henry MacCracken led NYU. He called college leaders together to talk about *reform*. Reform means changing rules to fix a problem.

words.d: the U.S. president who pushed colleges to make football safer in 1905
changing rules or ways of doing things to fix a problem

lessons.title: A Rule Body Called the NCAA
lessons.mainIdea: The 1905 crisis led to a new college rule body in 1906, renamed the NCAA in 1910, and to the forward pass becoming legal.
reading: Henry MacCracken's meetings led to a new group. In March 1906 it was formally set up as the *Intercollegiate Athletic Association of the United States*. About sixty colleges joined at the start.

In 1906 the rule makers changed football. They made the *forward pass* legal. They also made a team gain ten yards, not five, to keep the ball. Leaders hoped these changes would break up the dangerous piles.

In 1910 the group took a new name: the National Collegiate Athletic Association, or *NCAA*. Today the NCAA runs rules and championships for many college sports. It began because of a safety crisis in one game.

lessons.title: A Conference Born in Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: In 1895 leaders of seven Midwest universities met in Chicago and started the conference now called the Big Ten.
reading: In January 1895, the presidents of seven universities met at the Palmer House hotel in Chicago. They came from Chicago, Illinois, Michigan, Minnesota, Northwestern, Purdue and Wisconsin. They wanted shared rules for college sports.
Their group became the Western Conference. A *conference* is a group of schools that play each other under shared rules. Today it is known as the Big Ten.

*Amos Alonzo Stagg* coached football at the University of Chicago from 1892 to 1932. The school's field was named Stagg Field. Chicago left the conference in 1946, but it was one of the group's first members.

words.d: a group of schools that play each other under shared rules

lessons.title: A Stadium That Remembers
lessons.mainIdea: Memorial Stadium at the University of Illinois was built as a memorial to people who died in World War I.
reading: After World War I, the University of Illinois raised money for a new stadium in Champaign. Students, graduates and neighbors gave donations. The first game there was in 1923.
The stadium is called *Memorial Stadium*. Its columns carry the names of Illinois students and graduates who died in the war. A *memorial* is a place or object built to remember people.

The stadium was dedicated on October 18, 1924. That day Red Grange of Illinois scored four touchdowns against Michigan in the first twelve minutes. The game made the new stadium famous across the country.

lessons.title: School Titles in Illinois
lessons.mainIdea: High school teams in Illinois played for city and conference titles for decades before the IHSA began state football playoffs in 1974.
reading: The *IHSA*, or Illinois High School Association, was founded in 1900. It runs contests between high schools across the state. For many years, though, it held no football playoffs. Teams played for conference titles instead.

Chicago had its own big game, the *Prep Bowl*. The Chicago Public League champion played the Catholic League champion. The 1937 game was held at Soldier Field. Its crowd is often reported as more than 100,000 people.
The IHSA held its first state football playoffs in 1974. Schools were grouped by size into classes. Today the IHSA crowns football champions in eight classes each fall.
